2017_107_051617mtg.paragraph: Agenda packet for the Troy Board of Education regular meeting of May 16, 2017 at the Services Building — the district's annual recognition-and-retirement meeting. It honors 16 Outstanding Support Staff nominees, 27 retirees whose service reaches back to 1974, a $10,000 AT&T Foundation grant funding transportation for after-school tutoring, and 80 TFEE mini-grants. It appoints Jessica Carrier Special Education Supervisor from 135 applicants and Elizabeth Soggs Director of Technology from 34, approves a copier lease at not more than $63,690.48 per year, and takes a first reading of five board policies.

**Meeting**
Regular meeting, May 16, 2017, 7:00 PM, Services Building, 4420 Livernois.

**Recognition — six items**

The Mission Moment honors Barnard teacher **Taryn Huang**, accepted into Columbia University's Teachers College August Writing Institute — a program for educators "committed to turning classrooms into richly literate reading and writing workshops," admitting only a small number of applicants each year.

The accompanying presentation traces what the district has already built from the same partnership. The Teachers College Reading and Writing Project is a think tank started at Columbia under Lucy Calkins. Hamilton principal **Sarah Glasser** and Hill literacy specialist **Erin Detmer** attended the January Writing Coaching Institute; the presentation quotes John Hattie — "I suggest that we should focus on the greatest source of variance that can make the difference – the teacher." Back in Troy, Glasser began working shoulder to shoulder with teachers as a coach, the takeaway being that coaching is powerful **because teachers get feedback in the midst of instruction**, so every day becomes an opportunity for professional growth. Detmer set up lab experiences at Hill where the coach models a strategy and the teacher tries it in a safe environment. Curriculum and Instruction Specialist **Natalie Haezebrouck** observed both and carried the strategies into CAT network meetings — "giving teachers time to practice makes learning 'sticky!'" The three then created a three-day **Troy Coaching Institute** for principals and literacy specialists, working in classrooms with students at Hamilton and Hill.

Sixteen support staff were nominated for the Outstanding Support Staff Award, chosen by people "who talked about the impact these employees have on the lives of those around them… when we say we ensure learning for all, ALL truly means ALL." **Erin Prendergast**, para/resource room at Troy Union, is named Employee of the Year and forwarded to the county for the Betty Campion Outstanding Support Staff Award.

Twenty-seven retirees are introduced, the longest-serving being **Gary Griffith, a teacher since 1974**, followed by Sharon Brennan (1977), Karen Hurst (1977), and Renee Fidler, Gary Mason and Valerie Pfeifer (all 1978). Monitors display a visual recognition for twenty minutes beforehand; Jordan Harris reads each name, position and length of career, and **Board Vice-President Karl Schmidt** presents each a clock.

The fourth item recognizes a **$10,000 grant from the AT&T Foundation**, secured through the Troy Community Foundation and Oakland County Commissioner Doug Tietz, used to provide **transportation for high school students in after-school tutoring programs**. The fifth recognizes the Troy Foundation for Educational Excellence, which **funded 80 grants** this year, with president Julie McClure presenting. The sixth adopts a resolution supporting National Teacher Appreciation Week, May 8-12, 2017.

**Consent agenda**
Minutes of the April 11 workshop and April 18 meeting, the March 2017 Treasurer's Report, and approval of the 2017-2018 Oakland ISD budget.

**Treasurer's Report — March 2017**
Total check disbursements are $10,608,683.41, the General Fund group $8,236,384.18 and the General Fund (101) itself $7,796,483.29. Adding $2,029,494.15 of wire transfers, $167,542.09 of P-Card purchases and $50,038.72 of ACH debits, less $5,305.96 of prior period voids, total disbursements in period are $12,850,452.41.

**Personnel — two appointments, two very different fields**

**Jessica Carrier**, Special Education Supervisor, effective July 1, 2017. An 18-year career: middle school special education teacher at Fraser Public Schools, then assistive technology consultant, teacher consultant, middle school assistant principal and principal there, and for the last two years Director of Special Education at Fraser. She holds a B.A. in special education from Central Michigan, a master's in educational administration and a specialist degree in educational leadership from Saginaw Valley State, plus Director of Special Education state certification. **135 applications, 11 first-round interviews, 4 finalists** — Carrier, Michelle Flessa (TSD special education teacher), Lydia Moore (Oakland Schools early childhood special education consultant) and Sarah Young (TSD behavior support coordinator).

**Elizabeth Soggs**, Director of Technology, effective June 5, 2017. A 17-year career: technical systems coordinator at Bloomfield Hills, executive director of technology for the School District of the City of Pontiac, and for the last seven years Director of Technology and REMC 6 at Bay-Arenac ISD — where she led the district from the E-rate service provider role to that of an internet services consortium, provided project leadership for 13 districts selecting and implementing a new student management system, and created the "REMC 6 Tech Group" of teachers from three counties. **34 applications, 10 first-round interviews, 4 finalists.**

(The Carrier item's closing line reads "Ms. Carrier will begin her duties as Director of Technology" — text carried over from the Soggs item; the resolution correctly says Special Education Supervisor.)

**Business**
Following last year's Technology and Business Services review of copiers and installations, the Board authorizes Phase 2: a Master Equipment Lease Agreement with **Great America Financial Services** for a fleet of copiers, term no greater than four years, **not to exceed $63,690.48 per year**; and a Cost per Copy Maintenance Agreement with **Applied Imaging** not to exceed **$.0032 per impression for Canon monochrome** and **$.0049 black and $.059 color for Canon color equipment**, also up to four years, from the General Fund. The attached schedule places an IR 8595i in the workroom of each elementary at **$379.11 monthly**.

**Other**
First reading of board policies **2000.04** School District Clubs & Other Activities, **4000.01** Personnel – Labor Negotiation Team, **5000.03** Purchasing – Competitive Bidding & Micro-Purchases, **6000.02** Safety & Security – Firearms & Other Weapons, and **8000.09** General Policies – Web Accessibility, reviewed by the Board's attorney for compliance with state law, the Open Meetings Act and the Revised School Code. Adoption is set for the June 6 meeting. (The agenda index and item heading list four policies; the body lists five, adding 5000.03.)

Agenda packet for the regular meeting of the Troy School District Board of Education, May 16, 2017, 7:00 PM at the Services Building, 4420 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098. The agenda is: 1. Pledge of Allegiance; 2. Recognition — A. TSD Mission Moment: Teachers College, B. Outstanding Support Staff Person of the Year, C. Troy School District Retirees, D. AT&T/Troy Community Foundation Grant Award, E. TFEE Grant Award Winners, F. Teacher Appreciation Week; 3. Additions & Deletions; 4. Public Communication (agenda items); 5. General – Consent Agenda — A. Minutes of the April 11, 2017 Board of Education Workshop, B. Minutes of the April 18, 2017 Board of Education Meeting, C. Treasurer's Report – March 2017, D. Approve 2017-2018 Oakland Intermediate School District Budget; 6. Personnel — A. Consideration: Administrative Appointment – Special Education Supervisor, B. Consideration: Administrative Appointment – Director of Technology; 7. Curriculum; 8. Business — A. Consideration: Copier Lease (Elementary, IA-East & TCCHS); 9. Public Communication (non-agenda items); 10. Other — A. First Reading: Board Policies; 11. Adjournment. Meetings are cablecast on TS-TV Channel 19 (Comcast) and Channel 15 (WOW) every Monday and Wednesday at 2:00 and 9:00 p.m. when school is in session, and viewable at http://vimeo.com/troyschools. Two recognition item headers carry the date stamp 05.17.16 rather than 05.16.17, unrevised from the prior year's packet.

**Recognition 2.A: Teachers' College.** The Board honors Barnard Elementary teacher Taryn Huang, accepted into the prestigious Teachers' College at Columbia University August Writing Institute. The Writing Institute is designed for educators, classroom teachers, school administrators and curriculum specialists who are committed to turning classrooms into richly literate reading and writing workshops; applicants must apply and only a small number are accepted each year. Huang is invited up to describe what she hopes to learn and bring back to Troy, and receives a certificate after she speaks.

The accompanying presentation, titled "University of Columbia, Teachers College Partnership: Building Capacity In TSD," sets out what the district has already built from the relationship. The Teachers College Reading and Writing Project is described as a think tank started at Columbia University under the leadership of Lucy Calkins, whose mission is to help young people become avid readers, writers and inquirers through effective instruction, working shoulder to shoulder with educators at all levels to hone literacy practices.

Under the heading "Investing in Learning: Coaching Institute at TCRWP," the presentation quotes John Hattie — "I suggest that we should focus on the greatest source of variance that can make the difference – the teacher" — and records that Sarah Glasser, Hamilton principal, and Erin Detmer, Hill literacy specialist, attended the January Writing Coaching Institute, where they learned a model for supporting teachers to provide responsive, evidence-based instruction in literacy.

Back at Troy, Glasser immediately started working shoulder to shoulder with teachers in the role of coach. The Teachers College takeaway recorded is that the role of coach is a powerful one because teachers get feedback while in the midst of instruction, so that every day becomes an opportunity for professional growth; Hamilton teachers have been honing their ability to deliver effective one-on-one conferences. At Hill, Detmer set up lab experiences in which the coach models a strategy and then the teacher tries it out in a safe environment, the takeaway being that professional learning should be frequent and provide opportunities for immediate practice.

Natalie Haezebrouck, Curriculum and Instruction Specialist for Elementary Literacy, observed both Detmer and Glasser and used strategies from the Coaching Institute at CAT meetings to make teacher learning more authentic — "giving teachers time to practice makes learning 'sticky!'" The three then created a three-day Troy Coaching Institute for principals and literacy specialists, in which participants worked in classrooms with students at Hamilton and Hill to hone their craft.

The structure of the item is worth noting: the Board is not merely congratulating one teacher on an acceptance, it is showing the return on two earlier acceptances — a single January institute attended by two staff, propagated through a building principal, a literacy specialist, a district curriculum specialist and finally a three-day institute for the district's own principals.

**Recognition 2.B: 2016-17 Outstanding Support Staff Award.** Sixteen individuals were nominated, chosen by colleagues, parents and students who talked about the impact these employees have on the lives of those around them: "They exemplify our values and help us to ensure that when we say we ensure learning for all, ALL truly means ALL."

The nominees are Rose Arnon, custodian, Costello; Nahla Asmar, ELD tutor, Boulan Park; Margaret Baines, facility manager, Athens; Dawn Copp, health care aide, Martell; Janet Davert, secretary, Baker; Maxine Japowicz, paraprofessional, Martell; Janie Kirchler, health care aide, Hamilton; Sharon Kreza, secretary, Wattles; Ivonne Mastracci, secretary, Troy Union; Karyn Mroczka, secretary, Smith; Sue Ohlert, secretary, Athens; Joni Pallas, paraprofessional, special education, Larson; Candy Parker, bus driver; Erin Prendergast, para/resource room, Troy Union; Betty Prospal, secretary, employee services; and Seth Wyatt, paraeducator, special education, Costello.

From that pool, Erin Prendergast was awarded the Troy School District Outstanding Support Staff Employee of the Year, and her name was also sent to the county for consideration for the county-wide Betty Campion Outstanding Support Staff Award.

**Recognition 2.C: Troy School District retirees.** The item introduces employees who have retired or expressed their intention to retire at the end of the 2016-2017 school year, noting that not all could be present.

The retirees are Joan Barrett, teacher, Troy High, since 1987; Sharon Brennan, teacher, Larson Middle School, since 1977; Dikki CieChanski, teacher, Martell, since 1987; Mary Curl, secretary, Morse, support staff since 1996; Janet D'Agostino, secretary, Troy Career Center, support staff since 2000; Vera Dorr, ELD paraprofessional, Wass and Costello, support staff since 1996; William Edwards, computer technician, Services, support staff since 1995; Renee Fidler, teacher, elementary music, since 1978; Karen Field, support staff since 1997; Gary Griffith, teacher since 1974; Renee Haraburda, teacher since 1988; Karen Hurst, teacher since 1977; Mary Johnson, teacher since 1991; Mary Klotz, support staff since 1997; Janet MacDonald, support staff since 1987; Susan Madej, support staff since 1999; Gary Mason, teacher, Baker Middle School, since 1978; Janice Meganck, secretary, International Academy East, support staff since 1997; Valerie Pfeifer, teacher, Troy High, since 1978; Heide Rosenberg, teacher, Troy High, since 1991; Sandra Sinnaeve, ELD paraprofessional, Troy Union, support staff since 2000; Kathleen Steinberger, ELD paraprofessional, Wattles, support staff since 2001; Hank Thoenes, teacher, Boulan Park, since 1987; Colleen Tropea, teacher, Smith Middle School, since 1985; Camille Tucci, teacher, Athens, since 1986; and Linda Worrell, teacher, Troy High, since 1989.

The accompanying slides read "Thank you for the years of dedication and support you have given to the Troy School District. We wish you all the best in your retirement! Congratulations!" followed by a slide per retiree. Gary Griffith's forty-three years is the longest tenure in the group.

The staging instructions match those used in later years: for approximately twenty minutes before the board meeting all the monitors in the room display a visual recognition of the district's retirees; a note card is placed on a chair for each retiree attending; Jordan Harris reads each name, position and length of career; the retiree comes forward and stands near the presentation table; and the retirement gift, a clock, is presented — here by Board Vice-President Karl Schmidt rather than the president, Dr. Philippart.

**Recognition 2.D: AT&T Foundation grant award.** Earlier that fall, through the efforts of the Troy Community Foundation and Oakland County Commissioner Doug Tietz, the Troy School District received a $10,000 grant from the AT&T Foundation. The grant has been used to provide transportation for high school students who participate in after-school tutoring programs. Commissioner Tietz and a representative from the AT&T Foundation attend to describe the grant. The specific use is worth noting — the barrier the money removes is not the tutoring itself but getting home afterward.

**Recognition 2.E: TFEE mini-grant recipients.** The Board recognizes the Troy Foundation for Educational Excellence and the work it does to support the schools, students and staff. This year the Foundation funded 80 grants for a diverse group of projects to help enhance learning for students and enrich their educational opportunities. The Foundation is made up of volunteers who give of their time and talents to raise money for innovative projects that would not be possible without the resources TFEE provides. Julie McClure, president of the Foundation, briefly recognizes the most recent group of grant recipients, with names of recipients and projects displayed on screen.

**Recognition 2.F: National Teacher Appreciation Week.** Teacher Appreciation Week was celebrated May 8 through May 12, 2017. The resolution recites that throughout Troy and across the country teachers inspire, nurture and open children's minds to new ideas; that teachers promote and strengthen the principles of democratic equality, develop leaders and encourage critical thinking; that Troy teachers set the bar for excellence in education and continually exceed the highest standards in the profession; and that the goal of Teacher Appreciation Week is to raise national and local awareness of teaching excellence in building a better society — resolving that the district supports National Teacher Appreciation Week, May 8-12, 2017.

**Consent agenda.** Minutes of the April 11, 2017 Board of Education Workshop; minutes of the April 18, 2017 Board of Education Meeting; the Treasurer's Report for March 2017; and approval of the 2017-2018 Oakland Intermediate School District budget, the annual Section 624 review by which each constituent district expresses support or disapproval of the ISD's proposed budget.

**Treasurer's Report, March 2017.** General Fund (101) check disbursements are $7,796,483.29, with Total General Fund of $8,236,384.18 and TOTAL CHECK DISBURSEMENTS of $10,608,683.41. Adding ACH debits of $50,038.72, outgoing wire transfers of $2,029,494.15 and P-Card purchases of $167,542.09, and subtracting prior period void disbursements of $5,305.96, TOTAL DISBURSEMENTS IN PERIOD is $12,850,452.41. The middle sections of the packet are the March check register run by fund.

**Personnel 6.A: Special Education Supervisor.** The recommendation is Ms. Jessica Carrier, with an extensive 18-year career in education. She began as a middle school special education teacher for Fraser Public Schools, then served as the assistive technology consultant for special education in the Fraser School District; her career progressed to special education teacher consultant, then middle school assistant principal, then principal for Fraser Public Schools. For the last two years she has served as Director of Special Education at Fraser, managing and overseeing all special education services within the district. She holds a Bachelor of Arts in special education from Central Michigan University, a master's degree in educational administration from Saginaw Valley State University, a specialist degree in educational leadership, and Director of Special Education state certification from Saginaw Valley State.

The item's closing sentence reads that with the Board's approval "Ms. Carrier will begin her duties as Director of Technology as of July 1, 2017" — text carried over from the Soggs item that follows; the resolution itself correctly issues a two-year probationary administrative contract without tenure in the administrative position to Ms. Jessica Carrier, who will begin her duties as Special Education Supervisor effective July 1, 2017.

The selection funnel is published in full: there were 135 applications submitted, of which 11 were granted first round interviews — Rebecca Anders, Jessica Carrier, Karly DiDocha, Tamaran Dillard, Michelle Flessa, Thomas Harwood, Jennifer Lorence, Lydia Moore, Melanie Morey, Chris Olson and Sarah Young. Of those, 4 moved to the final round: Jessica Carrier, Director of Special Education at Fraser Public Schools; Michelle Flessa, special education teacher, Troy School District; Lydia Moore, early childhood special education consultant, Oakland Schools; and Sarah Young, behavior support coordinator, Troy School District. The final selection was Jessica Carrier. (The transition line reads "Of the 7 listed above, 4 moved to the final round" while eleven names are listed — an inconsistency in the source.)

Three of the eleven first-round interviewees recur later in these packets: Sarah Young would be appointed Special Education Supervisor herself in May 2018, Melanie Morey was already principal at Barnard, and Carrier would be promoted to Director of Special Education in July 2018.

**Personnel 6.B: Director of Technology.** The recommendation is Ms. Elizabeth Soggs, with an extensive 17-year career in the technology field. She began as a technical systems coordinator for the Bloomfield Hills School District, then served as executive director of technology for the School District of the City of Pontiac. For the last seven years she has served as Director of Technology and REMC 6 at Bay-Arenac Intermediate School District, where she fulfilled many additional responsibilities including leading the district from the E-rate service provider role to the role of an internet services consortium, providing project leadership for 13 districts in the selection and implementation process of a new student management system, and creating the "REMC 6 Tech Group" comprised of teachers from three counties. She holds a bachelor's degree in business administration and computer information systems from Walsh College and a master of arts in educational technology from Central Michigan University. The resolution issues a two-year probationary administrative contract without tenure in the administrative position, with duties beginning June 5, 2017.

The funnel: there were 34 applications submitted, of which 10 were granted first round interviews — Henry Christian, John Graham, Evan Humphrey, Matthew McCarty, Andrew Piazza, Nicholas Pitrone, Wesley Prescott, Elizabeth Soggs, Andrew Steinman and Gary van Staveren. Of those, 4 moved to the final round of interviews and building visits: Andrew Piazza, Director of Technology and Instructional Integration at Northville Public Schools; Wesley Prescott, Technology Coordinator–Field Services at Oakland ISD; Elizabeth Soggs, Director of Technology and REMC6 at Bay-Arenac ISD; and Gary van Staveren, building principal at Hamlin Elementary School, Rochester Community Schools. The final selection was Elizabeth Soggs.

The contrast between the two searches is stark and is visible only because the district publishes both funnels: 135 applicants for a special education supervisor's post against 34 for a technology directorship, in the same month, at the same district. Soggs's E-rate experience proved directly relevant — she is the Beth Soggs who would run the district's fiber maintenance and network equipment RFPs through 2018, both of them turning on E-rate reimbursement.

**Business 8.A: copier lease approval.** The previous year, Technology and Business Services conducted a review of copiers and installations. As a result, it is recommended the district enter into Phase 2 of lease and maintenance agreements.

The resolution authorizes the Superintendent or designee to negotiate and execute a Master Equipment Lease Agreement with Great America Financial Services for the purpose of leasing a fleet of copiers for a period no greater than four years at an annual cost not to exceed $63,690.48 per year. It further authorizes the Superintendent or designee to negotiate and execute a Cost per Copy Maintenance Agreement with Applied Imaging not to exceed $.0032 per impression for Canon monochrome equipment and $.0049 black and $.059 color per impression for Canon color equipment, for a period not to exceed four years, with these amounts approved as expenditures of the General Fund.

The attached 2017 schedule lists each site by address, location within the building and phone number, with the Applied new model number and Canon monthly lease amount. The elementary schools each take an IR 8595i at $379.11 monthly: Barnard at 3601 Forge in the workroom; Bemis at 3571 Northfield Parkway in the back office workroom; Costello at 1333 Hamman in the workroom; Hamilton at 5625 Northfield Parkway in the workroom; Hill at 4600 Forsyth Drive in the teacher workroom; Leonard at 4401 Tallman Drive in the staff workroom; Martell at 5666 Livernois in the staff workroom; and Morse at 475 Cherry Street in the teacher workroom.

**Other 10.A: first reading of board policies.** Members of the Board Policy Committee have reviewed board policies 2000.04 School District Clubs & Other Activities; 4000.01 Personnel – Labor Negotiation Team; 5000.03 Purchasing – Competitive Bidding & Micro-Purchases; 6000.02 Safety & Security – Firearms & Other Weapons; and 8000.09 General Policies – Web Accessibility. These policies have been reviewed by the Board of Education's attorney to ensure they comply with state law, the Open Meetings Act and the Revised School Code. The first reading of these revised and additional policies is presented at this meeting, and all Board members will be asked to review them a second time before the next meeting and vote on adoption under the consent agenda at the June 6 Board meeting.

The agenda index and the item heading both list four policies, omitting 5000.03; the body of the item lists five. The five-policy list is the operative one.

Read as a whole, the May 2017 packet is the district's annual accounting of its people. Twenty-seven employees leave, one of them after forty-three years; sixteen support staff and every teacher in the district are thanked; two administrative posts are filled from funnels the district publishes in full, showing 135 applicants for one and 34 for the other; and one teacher's acceptance to a Columbia institute is used to show what two earlier acceptances already produced — a coaching model that moved from an institute in January to two buildings, then to the district's curriculum specialists, then to a three-day institute Troy ran for itself.
